To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the first generation models (i.e., the balance-of-payments and the monetary models) are the most relevant to the case of transition countries; and (2) the second and third generation approaches are also useful in explaining the causes of currency crises in transition countries.
currency crises in transition economies are driven by a combination of macroeconomic, institutional, social and external factors.
the first generation variables are important, but not sufficient, to explain the occurrence of crises in foreign exchange markets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: what are the main determinants of currency crises in selected transition economies?
the identification and measurement of the determinants of currency crises in the context of transition economies.
the following question: which factors are important in explaining currency crises in the selected countries?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the causes of currency crises in transition economies are a complex mixture of factors, and the results of the analysis are in line with those of the previous studies, but the new approach is able to provide a more detailed picture of the causes and effects of currency crises.
currency crises in transition economies are the product of a combination of first, second and third generation factors, with the latter two playing a more important role than the first.
the first, second and third generation theories are all relevant and should not be considered as substitutes for each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most influential macroeconomic variables for currency turbulence are inflation, interest rates and exchange rate regime.
the CATREG models provide an additional and useful perspective on the causes of turbulence, and they can be used to complement the existing theoretical models.
the most important determinants of currency crises in transition economies are macroeconomic variables, followed by social development and institutional ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transition process, as well as the degree of economic and political liberalization, is a crucial factor in explaining currency turbulence in these countries.
the transition process is a long-term process, which needs a strong political will and a lot of effort in terms of economic and social development.
the transition process, which involves the introduction and development of a market economy, is a long process that is likely to be accompanied by currency turbulence.
